name: Deep Blue
lede: Deep blue is less a single color than a rank: the dark, saturated end of blue, a grade on the eighteenth-century dyers' scale and, since 1997, the name of a chess computer.

sections.title: A modifier, not a single color
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary remarks that when *deep* describes a color it means intense in hue, whereas in "the deep blue sea" the depth belongs to the ocean and not to the color [1]. Paterson also records that Deep Blue is the IBM supercomputer that beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in May 1997 [1].

The swatch here, #040273, is a very dark, saturated blue that leans slightly toward violet [2]. It comes from the xkcd color-name survey of 2010, and the ISCC-NBS charts of 1955 file it in block 170 [2]. The nearest ISCC-NBS name, deep purplish blue, lies 7.9 units away, and a near twin in the survey, Dark Royal Blue, is only 1.0 away [2]. Among familiar names, [[midnight-blue]] is 4.8 units from it, and the plain [[dark-blue]] of web colors is lighter and less violet [2].

Because *deep blue* is a description, history gives it many faces. The sections below follow the places where writers and dyers used the words for something specific.

sections.title: In antiquity
sections.body:
In *On Sense and Sensible Objects*, Aristotle names deep blue as one of five unmixed colors lying between light and dark, along with crimson, violet and leek-green and either grey or yellow [3]. In his *Meteorology* he lists only red, green and purple for the rainbow, so his attitude to blue is hard to pin down [4].

The Greek word most often translated as blue, *kyaneos*, stood for dark colors in the classical age, spanning deep blue, violet, brown and black [5]. In Homer's day it could mean an iris's bright blue or the black of mourning clothes, yet it was never applied to sky or sea [5]. Ball argues that to the Greeks blue was a kind of darkness, which fits the beards on Greek statues, painted a deep blue that was understood as a kind of black [4].

From such facts a nineteenth-century debate grew. William Gladstone even proposed that the Greeks had no word for blue because they could not see it [6]. That idea is wrong. Greek temples carried blue pigment, in backgrounds much darker than later drawings show, and Ball notes several Greek words that do translate as the blue of sky and sea [4][5]. The Greeks saw blue; they filed it largely under darkness [4].

sections.title: Stones and powders
sections.body:
For painters, a deep blue meant a material. Lapis lazuli is a stone whose deep blue is threaded with fine veins that ancient peoples believed were gold; they are in fact iron pyrite [5]. Marco Polo, who visited the mines in 1271, wrote of a mountain that yielded the finest blue [7]. The color comes from sulphur atoms in the mineral lazurite, which absorb red light [4].

The stand-ins were graded by cost. In *Saints Peter and Dorothy* of about 1505 to 1510, the Master of St Bartholomew painted Peter's deep blue robe in the highest grade of azurite and used a cheaper, greener grade for the cuffs, where finer particles gave a lighter shade [4]. Smalt, a ground cobalt glass, kept its strong deep blue only when left coarse, which made it gritty and hard to paint with [4][8]. The best grade had a purplish cast, and it was largely replaced by ultramarine [4][1].

Two accidents and a chemist's programme gave later blues. When Diesbach tried to concentrate a red lake made with tainted potash, it went purple and then deep blue, and that accident became [[prussian-blue]], available to artists by 1724 [4][8]. A fine deep blue came in 1802 when Thénard roasted cobalt arsenate or phosphate with alumina, the start of [[cobalt-blue]] [7]. Much older is [[egyptian-blue]], made by firing copper oxide, calcium carbonate and silica, and recreated by modern researchers, who needed three firings to get a deep blue mass of crystals; excavations at Tell el-Amarna had uncovered the ancient workshops [9].

sections.title: The dyers' ladder
sections.body:
In dyeing, deep blue was a grade. Balfour-Paul reports that eighteenth-century European dyers sorted indigo into thirteen shades, lightest first: milk-blue, pearl-blue, pale-blue, flat-blue, middling-blue, sky-blue, queen's-blue, Turkish-blue, watchet-blue, garter-blue, mazareen-blue, deep-blue, and infernal or navy blue [10]. Finlay gives the same ladder with twelve rungs, leaving out Turkish blue [11]. Either way, deep blue sits second from the darkest.

Two of those rungs became ordinary color words. Queen's blue, also called royal blue, and navy blue left the dye house behind [10]. You can meet them as [[royal-blue]] and [[navy]]. Deep blue is the rung that stayed a description.

The reward for depth was durability. A cloth dyed deep with [[indigo]] resists fading so well that it can survive for centuries, as the dark blue grounds of oriental carpets show [10]. In late Edo Japan, town and country dress alike was mostly dyed a deep blue [10]. Dark indigo was often judged better than black; certain Moroccan Berber shawls were priced by how much indigo, rather than black, their stripes contained [10].

sections.title: Newton's deep blue
sections.body:
Pastoureau says Newton first distinguished six rays in the spectrum and later added a seventh, a deep blue or "indigo", to make seven [12]. Finlay observes that indigo was then thought of as a dye rather than a color, and wonders which of the dyers' shades Newton might have had before him [11].

The number is the myth. The seven bands are not natural divisions of the rainbow, which grades smoothly. Newton chose seven to match the seven notes of the musical scale, as Ball and others explain [4][12]. Westland adds that Newton's blue and indigo would be called cyan and blue today [13]. His deep blue was whatever stood between the two, a name for a stretch of continuous light.

sections.title: Names and pictures
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary glosses a string of names with the same two words: imperial blue, jockey club, madonna blue, matelot blue, National blue and Sèvres blue are each simply "a deep blue" [1]. Smalt is called more often a deep blue than a pale one, and cerulean is "the deep blue colour of a cloudless sky" [1]. That last wording does not match the pigment cerulean blue, which the same book describes as a vivid light greenish blue discovered in 1860 [1]. [[imperial-blue]] and [[cerulean]] show how far the family stretches.

Painters and writers have used the plain phrase for effect. In the apse mosaic at St Catherine's, Sinai, as Gage describes it, the tunics of two apostles turn deep blue where Christ's rays strike them [14]. Renoir's *Boating on the Seine* of 1879 to 1880 sets an orange skiff against deep blue water, an opposition Ball reads as a deliberate play of complementaries [4]. The artist Joseph Cornell wanted his film *Rose Hobart* projected through a deep blue filter, and coined a word, "Blueaille", for the effect [15]. Jarman writes of the Japanese morning glory, a deep blue flower that opens at dawn and fades in sunlight [16].

Mid-century advice about film was cruder: Birren recommended cutting abruptly from deep blue to bright red for maximum excitement [17]. That is a period opinion, not a tested rule.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Deep blue as a painted color is rare. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only four works, all portraits from 1768 to 1813 [18]. They are [[painting:aic-16009|Portrait of Sarah Sophia Banks]] by Nathaniel Hone, [[painting:aic-7255|Portrait of Miss Braddon]] by George Engleheart, [[painting:aic-7443|Portrait of Marquerite du Chatelet]] by Peter Edward Stroely and [[painting:aic-7247|Portrait of Andre Liodet]] by R. Duparq [18]. In all four the match plays the darkest part of the picture, most likely a dark coat or ground, though we did not check what the patch is [18]. As always these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen color, not a pigment test [18].

The phrase *deep blue* is easier to chart than the paint. In Google Books it peaks around 1847, fell to about a quarter of that peak by 1980, and rebounded to half by 2000 [19]. The rebound coincides with the chess computer, but the data cannot separate the machine from the sea [19].
